message.content:
A common example of a **multinucleated** cell is a *skeletal‑muscle fibre* (also called a “myocyte” or “myofibre”).  
During development several individual muscle precursor cells—called **myoblasts**—fuse together to form one long tube. Each original nucleus remains inside this fused structure, so the resulting mature muscle fibre contains dozens (sometimes hundreds) of nuclei distributed along its length.

Other well‑known multinucleated cells include:

| Cell Type | Typical Function |
|-----------|------------------|
| **Osteoclast** | Bone-resorbing macrophage-like cells – each has many nuclei from fusion of monocytes/macrophages. |
| **Placental Syncytiotrophoblast** | Forms part of the placental barrier; arises from fusion of cytotrophoblast layers. |
| **Polykaryotic Giant Cells** | Found in granulomas during chronic inflammation; formed by fusion of activated macrophages. |

So when you hear “a cell with multiple nuclei,” think of a multinucleated or polynuclear cell such as a skeletal‑muscle fibre or an osteoclast.
